clean_story:
Memory under pressure. Stress reshapes recall.

The term comes from how the brain prioritizes survival over storage when threatened. A calm mind files memories like books on a shelf, neat and accessible. Stress scatters them like leaves in a storm—some lost, some stuck in the branches. The hormone cortisol, released during stress, floods the amygdala, the brain’s alarm center. This disrupts the hippocampus, where memories form. High cortisol can shrink hippocampal neurons, making recall harder. Yet mild stress can sharpen focus, like a spotlight on a stage. Soldiers in training often remember drills better under controlled stress. But chronic stress erodes memory: students cramming for exams with high anxiety often blank out. Tests show stressed subjects recall 20 percent fewer details than relaxed ones.

Three related subjects are memory consolidation, cortisol effects and emotional memory.
